p: The cat of Norse legend. A mountain-climbing giant in a weatherproof coat.
s: The Norwegian Forest Cat, called the Wegie for short, is the stuff of Viking legend. These big longhairs have lived in Norway for centuries, and they appear in Norse myth as the cats that pulled the goddess Freya's chariot. King Olav V named the breed the official cat of Norway.

It is built for a cold, wet climate. A long double coat with a dense woolly underlayer sheds rain and snow, topped by a full ruff, tufted lynx-tipped ears, and a long bushy tail. Big and muscular, the Wegie is a powerful climber that descends trees head-first.

For all its wild looks, the temperament is gentle and friendly. The Norwegian Forest Cat is calm, patient, and sociable, fond of its family without being demanding, and happy to watch the household from a high perch.

It is often confused with the Maine Coon, and the two share a similar size and rugged build, but they developed an ocean apart and differ in head shape and coat. The Wegie is slow to mature, reaching full size at around five years.

The Wegie is a calm, friendly giant that likes to survey its home from up high. It is sociable without being clingy, patient with children and other pets, and content to spend part of the day on its own, though it enjoys company when it is offered.

The water-shedding double coat needs regular brushing, with a heavy molt in spring that calls for daily attention. The breed is sturdy but can carry the heart condition HCM, a kidney condition, and a rare metabolic disorder called GSD IV, so reputable breeders test for them.
rc: Norway's legendary forest cat, in CFA's top fifteen
f: Origin of the Name
Named for the forests of Norway, where it lived for centuries, and tied to Norse myth as Freya's cat.
A Natural Breed
An ancient Scandinavian forest cat shaped by climate, later named the national cat of Norway.
Good to Know
Sociable and easygoing, it loves to climb and perch. The thick coat needs regular brushing, especially in spring.
Coat & Color
A long, water-shedding double coat with a ruff, tufted ears, and bushy tail, in many colors and patterns.
By the Numbers
Reaches full size at around five years. Similar to the Maine Coon but a distinct, separately developed breed.
Living with One
Offer tall perches, regular brushing, and easygoing company. The Wegie is independent but affectionate on its own terms.
Health Notes
Can carry the heart condition HCM and a rare metabolic disorder, so choose breeders who screen their lines.
d: The Norwegian Forest Cat wears a waterproof coat over a wool undercoat.
Norse myth gave the goddess Freya a chariot pulled by two giant cats.
It takes up to five years to reach full size and full glory.
Nothing says winter like a Wegie asleep in the hay, tail over its nose.
The best seat in the barn is the doorway, with a view and no wind.
King Olav V is said to have made it Norway's official cat. Ask your friends.
After the snow and the chores, a Wegie tucks in one paw and sleeps.
lw: The path is white and the cabin light is on.

A Norwegian Forest Cat has crossed this snow a thousand times. It walks without hurry, tail high, as if the forest were its own front yard. When it reaches the door, it does not ask to come in. It waits, because it knows the warm room is already waiting for it.

p: France's smiling blue. A quiet, woolly cat with a monastery legend.
s: The Chartreux is France's own blue cat, old enough to come wrapped in legend. Stories tie it to the Carthusian monks of the Grande Chartreuse, and it has been part of French life for centuries, praised by writers and treated as a national treasure.

The coat is its trademark. A dense, woolly, water-resistant blue-grey coat stands slightly away from the body, and a rounded head with full cheeks and a gently upturned mouth gives the breed its famous smile. Bright copper or orange eyes complete the look.

It is a robust, powerful cat on surprisingly fine legs, sometimes described as a potato on toothpicks. The Chartreux is an excellent mouser, calm and observant, and notably quiet, with some individuals barely making a sound.
The temperament is gentle and undemanding. Chartreux are devoted but reserved, attaching to their families while keeping a dignified, easygoing calm, content to follow quietly from room to room.

The Chartreux is a quiet, gentle companion that bonds closely while keeping a dignified calm. It is an excellent, patient mouser, content to follow its people from room to room and settle nearby, and it is notably silent, with some cats barely making a sound.

The dense, woolly coat is best cared for by combing and hand-grooming rather than heavy brushing, which can spoil its texture, and it sheds seasonally. The breed is robust and long-lived, though some lines can carry hip problems and a urinary tendency, so reputable breeders screen and owners keep it lean.
rc: France's ancient blue cat, with a woolly coat and a quiet smile
f: Origin of the Name
Linked by legend to the Carthusian monks of the Grande Chartreuse in France.
An Ancient Breed
A centuries-old French cat, celebrated in literature and regarded as a national treasure.
Good to Know
Calm, quiet, and devoted, it bonds closely while staying undemanding. A fine, observant mouser that rarely makes noise.
Coat & Color
A dense, woolly, water-resistant blue-grey coat with copper or orange eyes and a smiling expression.
By the Numbers
Robust and powerful on fine legs, and one of the quietest of all breeds.
Living with One
Comb the woolly coat by hand and offer calm company. The Chartreux is quiet, devoted, and easy to live with.
Health Notes
Hardy and long-lived, though some lines carry hip issues, so choose screened breeders and keep the cat lean and active.
d: The Chartreux is a French cat with a woolly blue coat and copper eyes.
Legend ties them to Carthusian monks of the Grande Chartreuse.
Many Chartreux seldom meow. A few never make a sound at all.
Any pot big enough will do. A Chartreux checks the fit and moves in.
Sit where the sun lands. Wait. The day will come to you.
They are called the smiling blue cats of France. Look at the mouth.
Even the busiest garden helper naps against the pots when work is done.
lw: The greenhouse glows and the frost is winning outside.

The Chartreux has made its rounds. It has checked every pot, every shelf, and every sunny square of floor. Now it settles on the burlap and lets the string lights count the hours. Tomorrow there will be more to inspect. Tonight, the smile stays.

p: Turkey's silken dancer. An elegant longhair with a national pedigree.
s: The Turkish Angora is one of the oldest known longhaired breeds, named for Ankara, the Turkish city once called Angora. It has charmed Europe since at least the 1600s, and Turkey treasures it enough to run a preservation program at the Ankara Zoo.

It is built for grace. A fine-boned, athletic body carries a silky single coat that flows when the cat moves, with a plumed tail and a delicate wedge-shaped face. The classic Angora is a brilliant white, often with eyes of blue, amber, or one of each.

The personality is lively and bold. Angoras are playful, clever, and athletic, fond of high perches and of being the center of attention, and they bond closely and follow their people from room to room.

One trait needs care. White, blue-eyed Angoras can carry a gene linked to deafness, especially on the blue-eyed side, so odd-eyed cats may hear on only one side. The single coat is silky and far easier to groom than a double one.

The Turkish Angora is a lively, bold cat that bonds closely and likes to be in charge of the room. It is playful and athletic, fond of high perches and water, and so attached to its people that it follows them about and tends to choose a favorite.

The silky single coat has no dense undercoat, so it rarely mats and needs only weekly brushing. The breed is generally healthy, but white, blue-eyed cats can carry a gene linked to deafness, and some lines carry the heart condition HCM and a rare neurological disorder, so reputable breeders test.
rc: Turkey's ancient national longhair, a treasure of the Ankara Zoo
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Ankara, the Turkish capital once called Angora, its home for centuries.
An Ancient Breed
One of the oldest longhairs, prized in Europe since the 1600s and preserved today in Turkey.
Good to Know
Active and attention-loving, it enjoys climbing and play. The single coat is easy to groom, with no dense undercoat to mat.
Coat & Color
A long, silky single coat with a plumed tail, classically pure white, also in many colors and patterns.
By the Numbers
White blue-eyed cats can carry a deafness gene, so odd-eyed Angoras may be deaf on the blue-eyed side.
Living with One
Give it heights, play, and attention. The Angora is bold and devoted and likes to run the household.
Health Notes
White blue-eyed cats can be deaf. Some lines carry the heart condition HCM, so choose breeders who screen their cats.
d: Angora is the old name for Ankara, the Turkish capital. This is the Ankara cat.
The Ankara Zoo runs a preservation program for the breed.
The silky coat has no dense undercoat, so it rarely mats.
A white cat in a white blanket is a magic trick. Look for the eyes.
Be elegant. Be curious. Stay near the sunniest window.
A white Angora may have one blue eye and one amber. Ask your friends.
The head goes down on the basket and the whole house gets quiet.
lw: The sunroom turns gold, and the snow outside turns rose.

The Turkish Angora has run, leapt, and inspected every lemon on the tree. Now the plume of a tail curls around it like a scarf. It has been loved in Ankara for centuries, and it knows exactly how to be admired. It only asks that the cushion stay warm.

p: A brick wrapped in silk. A glossy, golden-eyed cat that adores its people.
s: The modern Burmese traces to a single cat. In the 1930s a small brown cat named Wong Mau was brought from Burma to the United States, and a careful breeding program built an entire breed around her warm sable coat and sweet nature.

It is deceptively solid. The Burmese looks compact and rounded but feels surprisingly heavy in the hand, leading to the old description of a brick wrapped in silk. The short, glossy coat lies close to a muscular body, set off by large, round, golden-yellow eyes.

The temperament is its glory. Burmese are devoted, people-oriented, and endlessly affectionate, often called the most dog-like of cats for the way they follow, greet, and insist on laps. They stay playful and kittenish well into adulthood.
They do not like to be alone and thrive in busy, loving homes. The breed also helped create the Tonkinese through crosses with the Siamese, and it comes in sable and several diluted shades.

A Burmese is famously people-dependent. It wants laps, shoulders, and conversation, follows its owners from room to room, and stays playful and kitten-like for years, which makes it a delightful companion and a poor choice for anyone away from home all day.

The short, satiny coat needs only a weekly wipe, but the breed carries a few risks worth knowing, including dental disease, diabetes, and, in some lines, a serious skull deformity and a condition that causes painful sensitivity, so reputable breeders test carefully.
rc: The devoted sable cat descended from a single import named Wong Mau
f: Origin of the Name
Named for Burma, the homeland of Wong Mau, the foundation cat brought to the United States in the 1930s.
A Founding Cat
Nearly the entire breed descends from Wong Mau, bred to fix her warm brown coat and sweet temperament.
Good to Know
Affectionate and people-focused, it wants company and laps and dislikes being left alone for long.
Coat & Color
A short, satiny, close-lying coat, classically warm sable brown, also in dilute shades, with golden eyes.
By the Numbers
A parent of the Tonkinese through crosses with the Siamese, and a long-standing favorite for its dog-like devotion.
Living with One
Give it laps, play, and company. The Burmese is devoted and social and unhappy left alone for long stretches.
Health Notes
Easy to groom, but watch for dental disease and diabetes and choose breeders who screen for known inherited conditions.
d: Most Burmese cats trace back to one brown cat named Wong Mau.
Wong Mau came from Burma to the United States in the 1930s.
Burmese weigh more than they look. Fans call them bricks wrapped in silk.
Your journal is now a cat bed. Write around the cat.
A warm mug, a cold window, and one good view. That is enough.
A Burmese talks like a Siamese, only softer. Ask your friends.
A quilt, a fire, and a Burmese asleep on your side of the bed.
lw: The lamp is on, and the snow keeps falling.

The Burmese has followed you from room to room all week. It has sat on your book, your sweater, and your plans. Now it curls into the quilt with a sigh, content to be exactly where you are. A heavy little heart, warm all the way through.
